title: Frogs, and the cane toad

identification.basis: The dictionary has the general frog word, the green frog and an edible large frog. The Atlas of Living Australia records the green tree frog, Roth's tree frog, the desert tree frog, the New Holland frog, the ornate burrowing frog and others within 30 km of Karma Waters, and the cane toad five times within 30 km and over a thousand times within 60.

summary: **[yirku-yirku](word:yirku-yirku)** is a frog, **[karrkurr](word:karrkurr)** the green frog, and **[yuday](word:yuday)** a 'large frog, edible', which is the whole of what the dictionary says and enough: frogs were bait, food and the first sound of the wet [ref:hershberger1982]. At Bloomfield, 'bait was generally grubs, small freshwater prawns or small frogs' on the freshwater lines; on the lower Tully in flood people waded into the shallows with a stick and a dilly bag and took the green frogs 'dozens and dozens' at a time; and in the dry north-west frogs 'are usually dug up from their burrows' [ref:anderson1996] [ref:roth1901]. Within 30 km of [Karma Waters](place:karma-waters) the Atlas has the green tree frog, Roth's tree frog, the desert tree frog, the New Holland frog that sits out the dry underground, and the ornate burrowing frog [ref:ala-karma]. It also has the cane toad, five times within 30 km and 1,079 times within 60, which is the thing on this page to know first: it kills the dogs, the [goannas](entry:goanna) and the [snakes](entry:snakes) that eat it, and it is not a frog to touch or to eat [ref:ala-karma-60] [ref:wiki-cane-toads].

sections.heading: Names
sections.body: **[yirku-yirku](word:yirku-yirku)** 'frog'; **[karrkurr](word:karrkurr)** 'green frog'; **[yuday](word:yuday)** 'large frog, edible' [ref:hershberger1982]. The dictionary has no word for the cane toad, which reached Kuku Yalanji country long after the dictionary's speakers learned their words for frogs [ref:wiki-cane-toads].

sections.heading: The frogs of the upper Mitchell
sections.body:
**Green tree frog** (*Litoria caerulea*, *karrkurr*), two records within 30 km and seventy-nine within 60. 'Larger than most Australian frogs, the Australian green tree frog reaches 10 cm or more in length. Its average lifespan in captivity, about 16 years, is long compared with most frogs. Docile and well suited to living near human dwellings, Australian green tree frogs are often found on window sills or inside houses, eating insects drawn by the light.' 'A plump, rather large tree frog, and can grow up to 11.5 cm in length ... A distinctive fatty ridge is seen over the eye'. 'The call is a low, slow brawk-brawk-brawk, repeated many times. For most of the year, the frogs call from high positions, such as trees and gutters, but during the breeding season, they descend to near the ponds and pools, where they breed ... They are particularly vocal after rain'. 'They favour old stands of *Eucalyptus*, where the trees have hollows in which water collects'. 'The skin secretions of the frog have antibacterial and antiviral properties' [ref:wiki-green-tree-frog].

**Roth's tree frog** (*L. rothii*), the **desert tree frog** (*L. rubella*), the **bumpy rocket frog** (*L. inermis*), ***L. nigrofrenata*** and ***L. pyrina*** are the other tree frogs in the 30 km records: the small brown and grey frogs of the paperbarks, the grass and the camp tank, which come out in hundreds with the first storms [ref:ala-karma].

**New Holland frog** (*Cyclorana novaehollandiae*), one record within 30 km and forty-three within 60, with the striped burrowing frog and the short-footed frog. '*Cyclorana* inhabits some of the most arid zones of Australia. Some species burrow underground and remain dormant for more than 5 years to survive drought conditions. They can store large amounts of water in their bladders, and form a "cocoon" around themselves to reduce loss of water, so are often called "water-holding frogs". They only return to the surface to breed and eat, and normally only after heavy summer' rain [ref:wiki-cyclorana]. These are the big burrowing frogs of the flats, and the dictionary's *yuday*, 'large frog, edible', is likely one of them or the green tree frog [ref:hershberger1982]. The **ornate burrowing frog** (*Platyplectrum ornatum*), 157 records within 60 km, is the small round one that comes up in the sand after rain [ref:ala-karma-60].

**Cane toad** (*Rhinella marina*). Not a frog of this country at all: introduced to Queensland in 1935 and across the north since, poisonous at every stage from egg to adult. The goannas, the frog-eating snakes, the death adders, the quolls and the freshwater crocodiles that eat it die; dogs that mouth it die; the keelback is one of the few snakes that survives it [ref:wiki-cane-toads]. Five records within 30 km of the homestead and 1,079 within 60 [ref:ala-karma] [ref:ala-karma-60].

sections.heading: Frog or toad
sections.body:
- **Cane toad**: dry warty skin, a bony ridge over each eye, big swollen glands behind the head, sits upright and walks as much as hops; the tadpoles are small and black in shoals; the eggs in long jelly strings. No native frog here has the glands [ref:wiki-cane-toads].
- **Green tree frog**: smooth, bright to dull green, a fatty ridge over the eye, sticky toe pads, on tanks, trees and walls [ref:wiki-green-tree-frog].
- **Burrowing frogs**: round, smooth, mottled, with a shovel on the heel; found by digging, or out in numbers after storms [ref:wiki-cyclorana].
- **The small tree frogs**: brown, grey or pale, with toe pads, in the paperbarks and the grass [ref:ala-karma].
- **Rule**: a warty one with glands is a toad; leave it, and keep the dog off it [ref:wiki-cane-toads].

sections.heading: Signs
sections.body:
- **The first chorus after the first storm**: every frog in the country calling, and the red-bellied black and the keelback at the pools the next night [ref:wiki-green-tree-frog] [ref:wiki-rbbs].
- **A slow brawk-brawk from a tank or a hollow** on a dry night: the green tree frog [ref:wiki-green-tree-frog].
- **Black tadpole shoals** in a shrinking pool and jelly strings on the weed: cane toad [ref:wiki-cane-toads].
- **A burrow mouth in sand with a frog's shape pressed in it**, Roth's 'surface indications' of a buried frog [ref:roth1901].
- **Dead goannas and snakes** near water with nothing wrong with them but a toad inside [ref:wiki-cane-toads].

sections.heading: Where they live
sections.body: The tree frogs in the hollows of the old gums and the paperbarks by the [waterhole](entry:waterhole), the camp tank and the shed; the burrowing frogs under the sandy flats and the clay pans, down for the dry; the ornate burrowing frog in the river sand; all of them at the pools when they breed [ref:wiki-green-tree-frog] [ref:wiki-cyclorana] [ref:ala-karma-60]. The cane toad is everywhere the others are, and at the camp light every night [ref:wiki-cane-toads].

sections.heading: Frogs in the chain
sections.body: Frogs are the link between the insects and everything else: they eat the moths and ants at the light and the water's edge, and they feed the red-bellied black [snake](entry:snakes), the keelback, the [sleepy cod](entry:sleepy-cod), the kingfishers and the egrets, the [goannas](entry:goanna) and the [freshwater crocodile](entry:freshwater-crocodile) [ref:wiki-rbbs] [ref:wiki-cane-toads]. The cane toad has stepped into that link and poisoned it: the animals that ate frogs now eat toads and die, which is why goannas, death adders and quolls have crashed across the north where the toad has gone [ref:wiki-cane-toads]. The burrowing frogs are the river's drought bank, down in the clay with a bladder full of water for years, up for a week of rain to breed [ref:wiki-cyclorana].

sections.heading: Seasons
sections.body: The first storms of the build-up bring the frogs up and the chorus on; the wet is the breeding season at the pools; through the dry the tree frogs sit in the hollows and the tanks, 'particularly vocal after rain', and the burrowing frogs are underground [ref:wiki-green-tree-frog] [ref:wiki-cyclorana] [ref:bom-palmerville]. See [the year on country](entry:seasons).

sections.heading: Uses
sections.body:
- **Bait** for the freshwater [lines](entry:hooks-and-lines): 'grubs, small freshwater prawns or small frogs' [ref:anderson1996].
- **Food**: *yuday*, 'large frog, edible'; on the Tully the green frogs were taken 'dozens and dozens' in a flood; in the north-west dug from their burrows [ref:hershberger1982] [ref:roth1901].
- **A calendar and a weather sign**: the chorus says rain [ref:wiki-green-tree-frog].
- **A warning**: toads at the camp mean the dog on a lead at night [ref:wiki-cane-toads].

sections.heading: Taking frogs, and not taking toads
sections.body:
From Roth and Anderson [ref:roth1901] [ref:anderson1996]:

1. **Know the toad first.** Warts, glands behind the head, the upright sit: never a toad, never with bare hands if you can help it, and wash after [ref:wiki-cane-toads].
2. **Bait frogs**: the small tree frogs at the camp light or in the grass at the water's edge after dark, by hand [ref:anderson1996].
3. **The Tully flood method**: wade the shallows with a stick in the left hand and a bag over the shoulder; each frog caught with the right hand is struck on the stick and slung into the bag [ref:roth1901].
4. **Burrowing frogs**: in the dry, dig where the surface shows the burrow, by hand in sand, with the [digging stick](entry:digging-sticks) in hard ground [ref:roth1901].
5. **Cook** on the coals; a big *yuday* is a mouthful [ref:hershberger1982].

sections.heading: Safety
sections.body:
- Cane toads are poisonous to eat and to handle carelessly; the glands squirt; dogs die of mouthing them [ref:wiki-cane-toads].
- Frog-hunting at the water's edge at night is snake and crocodile time: a torch, a stick, boots, and someone watching [ref:crocwise] [ref:wiki-rbbs].
- Native frogs are protected wildlife in Queensland; native title holders taking them for personal, domestic or non-commercial communal needs are covered by section 211 of the *Native Title Act 1993* [ref:qld-nca] [ref:alrc].
- A green tree frog in the tank is cleaning it of mosquito larvae; leave it [ref:wiki-green-tree-frog].

sections.heading: On Country today
sections.body: The frogs still come up with the first storm at Karma Waters, and the green tree frog is in every tank and toilet on the station; the toad is at every light [ref:ala-karma-60] [ref:wiki-green-tree-frog]. Which frog is *yuday* is for the people who ate it; the contribution box below is for that [ref:hershberger1982].

sections.heading: Language
sections.body: *[yirku-yirku](word:yirku-yirku)* 'frog'; *[karrkurr](word:karrkurr)* 'green frog'; *[yuday](word:yuday)* 'large frog, edible'; *[bana](word:bana)* 'water'; *[bindimu](word:bindimu)* 'red bellied black snake', the frog's hunter [ref:hershberger1982].
